title: Can Trust in Science Be Improved? An Adaptive Experiment Testing Student-Designed Messages
summary: Can short messages raise trust in science? This registered adaptive survey experiment randomly assigned US adults recruited through Lucid to a pure control or one of 32 messages, including videos, texts, images and memes, many made by students. The outcome was trust in science after treatment, measured on a five-point scale. Of the 11,519 respondents, 8,572 were analysed. Five arms differed from control. The 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust by 0.17 points (95% CI [−0.26, −0.08], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' film lowered it by 0.10 (95% CI [−0.18, −0.02], p = 0.010). Three videos raised it by about 0.06 points each, with intervals that approach zero. For the other arms no difference was detected. Because 32 tests were left uncorrected and several arms are small,

extensions.label: Design advance
extensions.why: Addresses the design and power causes: it replaces bundled stimuli with a manipulated mechanism and concentrates sample on the one robust effect.
extensions.title: Decomposing the 'trust science too much' backfire
extensions.hypothesis: The original video lowers trust relative to control, and the drop is mainly due to the fallibility segment: the no-fallibility video and the neutral video will not lower trust, and the transcript will lower trust by a similar amount to the video.
extensions.primary_outcome: Post-treatment trust in science: mean of the 6-item scale (items 4-6 reverse-coded), 5-point.

extensions.label: Generalizability
extensions.why: Addresses the multiplicity and sample causes: a confirmatory replication of the three positive arms with a single correction, plus a test of where the effect holds.
extensions.title: Do the small positive videos replicate across samples and baseline trust?
extensions.hypothesis: Videos 12, 15 and 20 each raise post-treatment trust in science relative to control by about 0.06 points; effects differ by baseline trust (low vs high) and party identification.
extensions.primary_outcome: Post-treatment trust in science, mean of the 6 items with items 4-6 reverse-coded, adjusted for pre-treatment trust.

potential.verdict: A follow-up is worth running, but narrowly. Only the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video backfire (-0.17, p=0.0002) is robust to multiplicity. The three +0.06 effects are fragile, and the pipeline's completers check added no evidence. The retrieved literature is reporting-standards material, so no live empirical debate is visible and none is invented. Run the backfire decomposition first, since it has the largest effect and an explicit mechanism. Then run the larger replication of the positive videos, with stimulus documentation (the data brief) done in parallel at little cost.
